15 An electric car travels at a constant speed of 70 km h–1 for 80 km on a straight horizontal road and
uses energy E from its battery.
The total resistive force acting on the car is proportional to (speed)2. Assume that the electric
motor is 100% efficient.
How much energy is used from the battery when the car travels at a constant speed of 60 km h–1
for 80 km on the straight horizontal road?
A
0.73E
B
0.86E
C
1.2E
D
1.4E

hints: Notice the car is at constant speed on a horizontal road, so the motor force must exactly balance the total resistive force over the $80 \text{ km}$.
Connect the given $F$ proportional to $(\text{speed})^2$ to battery energy using work done $W = Fd$ with 100 percent efficiency.
Compare the two runs with a ratio for the same distance: new energy $= E \times (60/70)^2$ and evaluate the square.
walkthrough: At constant speed the resultant force is zero, so the forward driving force $F$ equals the total resistive force. The battery must supply the work done against this resistance.
Write the resistance law as $F = kv^2$, where $k$ is a constant and $v$ is speed in $\text{km h}^{-1}$.
With 100 percent efficiency, battery energy $=$ work done $= Fd = kv^2d$, where $d = 80 \text{ km}$ is the same for both journeys.
For the two speeds, divide the expressions so $k$ and $d$ cancel: $E_{60}/E = (60^2)/(70^2) = (6/7)^2$.
Calculate $(6/7)^2 = 36/49 \approx 0.73$, so $E_{60} \approx 0.73E$. This is option A.

A.explanation: Energy scales as $v^2$ for the same $80 \text{ km}$, so $(60/70)^2E = 0.73E$.

B.explanation: This uses $60/70$ to the first power, but resistive force is proportional to $(\text{speed})^2$ not speed.

C.explanation: This is the inverse ratio $(70/60)^2$, which would be the energy for going faster, not slower.

D.explanation: This is the inverse ratio $70/60$ to the first power and also predicts more energy at lower speed.
